title: Indra's net
hookLine: a net of jewels, each reflecting all the others

lines: A WINDOW TURNS INTO A MIRROR.
cards: At night, a window turns into a mirror.

Stand in a lit room and look out, and there you are, with the lamp behind you, and the lamp's reflection in the glass of a picture frame, and the frame in the window too: light bouncing from one surface into the next.
Most of the time nobody notices. Buddhist teachers tell of a net that does this on purpose, on a scale with no edges. It hangs over the palace of Indra, a king of the gods in old Indian stories.

teach.b: The picture is linked to the Avatamsaka Sutra, a Mahayana Buddhist scripture, and Buddhist teachers have opened it up step by step. First, the net.
It stretches out in every direction, with no edge, and at each knot where the threads cross hangs a jewel: clear, polished, shining. Second, the reflection.
Look closely into any one jewel, and you'll see in its surface all the other jewels of the net. Not one or two. All of them.
Third, the reflection inside the reflection.

teach.h: EACH ONE REFLECTS ALL THE OTHERS.
teach.b: Each of those reflected jewels is also reflecting all the others.

So in the one jewel you're looking at, you see the whole net, and inside every jewel in that picture, the whole net again, without end. One holds all, and all hold the one. Fourth, why the teachers use it.
It's a picture of how things are, they say.
Each thing is made of its connections, the way a jewel's whole look comes from what it reflects. Buddhist teaching calls this dependent arising: things come to be because of other things.
A modern Zen teacher, Thich Nhat Hanh, gave the idea a plainer name, interbeing, and pointed at a sheet of paper. In it, he said, you can see the tree, the rain, the logger, the sun.
Some teachers find a comfort in the net. No jewel is lost in a huge web. Each one is a place where the whole web shows up, the one next to it as much as any.

how: Buddhist teachers, especially in the Huayan and Zen traditions of East Asia, use Indra's net to teach dependent arising: that each thing exists through its connections to everything else.

o: an endless net of jewels, each one reflecting all
a fishing net the god Indra cast over the sea
a sacred map of the heavens over a palace

p: things come to be through other things

s: the net has one great jewel at its center
there's a jewel at each knot, and each one reflects all the others.
each reflected jewel is also reflecting all the others
the whole net, inside each reflection, without end.
the image teaches that each thing stands on its own
it teaches the opposite: nothing exists on its own.

games.q: you look closely into one jewel of Indra's net. what do you see?
o: the jewel next to it, and nothing else.
all the other jewels, each reflecting all the rest.
games.why: every jewel shows the whole net, and inside each reflection, the whole net again.

practice: Find something shiny near you, the back of a spoon, a glass of water, a dark screen, and look into its surface without counting: the lamp, a corner of the room, your own face, bent and small.
Turn it a little and watch a whole new room slide in, and let it be a jewel in the net, holding everything around it. If you pray, you can give thanks for any of what you see.

wordCard.voice: Indra's net. A Buddhist image: an endless net with a jewel at each knot, each jewel reflecting all the others. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: each reflects all. A jewel at every knot, and the whole net in each. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Thich Nhat Hanh, on interbeing (the sheet of paper)
